prize_parts.citation: for a poetry that turns collective catastrophe and personal ordeal into memorial form, extending the lyric sequence to the scale of landscape and public memory

statement.case_for: My opening preference for Zurita rests on literary grounds that the colleagues' opening statements have not displaced. The case is that the long sequences (Purgatory, Anteparadise and the later books) have an unmistakable voice. It is hallucinatory, elegiac and severe, and it is held together by a formal ambition that few living poets attempt: the sequence conceived as a single, cumulative structure rather than a set of separate lyrics. The work carries historical catastrophe into lyric language without becoming testimony or protest, because the claim to merit sits in the syntax, the imagery and the architecture of the books. The oeuvre spans more than four decades and shows sustained intensity, so it meets the criterion of depth and durability. It also bears on the idealist direction of Nobel's will through the depth of its imaginative and moral vision, not through its political symbolism. Can Xue (B001) remains my close second choice. Her dream-logic fiction is a rigorously maintained formal project, and I would accept her as a recommendation on literary merit. Adonis (B016) is a third option, given the reshaping of a poetic language across a very long career.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that poetry of this kind is the hardest genre to assess through translation, and the effect of Zurita's Spanish reaches non-Spanish readers only in part, including readers on this committee. A second reservation, raised by several colleagues, is that part of his fame rests on non-textual acts such as sky-writing and the desert inscription. The committee must not credit those as literature, and they must not lend the poems a reputation the verbal work has not earned. There is also a legitimate question whether the later volumes sustain the intensity of the first sequences. Finally, the historical subject matter risks dominating the reception, which would be a political rather than a literary basis for the award.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Can Xue first for a rigorously maintained dream logic and ranks Zurita fifth. She is unsure how far non-textual interventions should count within the framework of Nobel's will, and she notes that non-Spanish readers depend heavily on translators.
responses.response: I share the doubt about non-textual interventions, and I think it should be settled in the citation itself. A citation resting on the books of poetry keeps the sky-writing and desert works as context and leaves them out of the claim to merit, as my citation does. On translation we are in the same position with Zurita as with Adonis, whom she ranks second. The remedy is the same: weigh translators, regional expertise and commentary openly, and do not treat difficulty of rendering as evidence against the work. I agree with her that Can Xue's method is formally rigorous, and that is why she remains my alternative.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for visionary, densely patterned prose at very large scale, and Can Xue second. She asks whether Can Xue's allegorical dream method sustains variety across the whole oeuvre, and whether the maximalism of Cărtărescu repeats itself in very long books.
responses.response: Her question about variety in Can Xue is fair, and I cannot settle it from the supplied description. It is the main reason I do not move her to first place. I take the same test to Cărtărescu. His Blinding trilogy and Solenoid are large and powerfully individual, and I ranked him fourth because the question of originality beyond a clear Romantic and modernist lineage is still open for me. Scale and density are not in themselves sustained quality. A poet's sequence and a novelist's cycle have to be judged by whether each section earns its length. I find Zurita's sequences more tightly built on that test, though I hold the view with caution, since I read the novels only through translation.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first as an encyclopedic visionary prose project. He notes that Zurita's landscape-scale works lie largely outside the text, and that it is uncertain whether the later work sustains the earliest sequences' intensity and variety.
responses.response: I accept the second point and cannot answer it fully. The later volumes need the committee's closer attention before a recommendation is final, and I would want the regional expert reading to speak to it. On the first point, I would put it differently. The extra-textual works are real, but they extend a poetics that already exists in the books. They do not replace it. The visionary register he praises in Cărtărescu is, in my reading, also central to Zurita, where it is condensed into verse and a compressed sequence rather than spread through very long prose. The difference between the two is real, and I do not think the density of the longer form settles it in Cărtărescu's favour.

responses.point: Sward ranks Can Xue first and Robinson second, and places Zurita sixth. She notes that part of Zurita's force lies in acts and installations that are hard to weigh as literature, and that political and historical significance must be kept apart from verbal achievement.
responses.response: I agree with the principle and would apply it to every candidate on the list, Zurita included. My own test is whether the case survives once the Chilean context is set aside, and I think it does. The formal handling of the sequence and the visionary language are what justify the recommendation. I disagree in part on Robinson. Her sentence-level control is considerable, but I rank her below Zurita because the fiction is compact and the thematic range narrow, which I find a more serious limit on depth and breadth of oeuvre than the translation difficulty we would face with a poet.

uncertainties: Translation: the density and sound of Zurita's Spanish reach readers in Swedish and English only partly, so my assessment of his language is mediated by translators and commentary.
How the non-textual interventions should be treated in a citation under Nobel's will is not settled, and I treat them only as context.
Whether the later volumes sustain the intensity and variety of the early sequences is not verified, and I do not claim independent verification of the corpus.
For Can Xue, the degree of variation within a very consistent method across the whole oeuvre, and the partial English-language coverage of her corpus, remain unresolved.

Regional expert reports on Spanish-language, Chinese-language and Arabic-language poetry and fiction are not part of the supplied evidence, so comparative judgments across languages remain provisional.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My scholarly work on modern poetry, the fragment and exile literature is context and does not establish a connection to any shortlisted writer, and the profile records no personal or professional tie to any of them.
